Pursuant to Rule 207(a)(2) of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.207(a)(2) (2026), Pacific Gas
and Electric Company (“PG&E”) respectfully submits this Petition for Declaratory Order
(“Petition”) requesting approval of two transmission rate incentives for its project work
associated with thirteen transmission projects approved in the 2025-2026 Transmission
Plan of the California Independent System Operator Corporation (“CAISO”).
Specifically, PG&E is requesting that it be authorized to: (1) recover 100% of its
prudently incurred costs for its work associated with the thirteen projects if the projects
are cancelled or abandoned for reasons beyond PG&E’s control; and (2) include 100% of
the Construction Work In Progress in transmission rate base during the construction
period for nine of the thirteen projects.

PG&E is requesting approval within 60 days of the filing so PG&E can confidently move
forward with project planning activities in 2027, including permitting, engineering, and
procurement of long-lead materials needed to support project schedules.

         Pursuant to Section 219 of the Federal Power Act (FPA), 1 Rule 207 of the Rules
of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission), 2
the Commission’s Order No. 679, 3 and the Commission’s 2012 Policy Statement, 4
Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) respectfully requests two transmission rate
incentives for its project work associated with thirteen transmission projects (PG&E
Projects) approved in the 2025-2026 Transmission Plan of the California Independent
System Operator Corporation (CAISO). Specifically, PG&E is requesting that it be
authorized to: (1) recover 100% of its prudently incurred costs for its work associated
with the thirteen projects if the projects are cancelled or abandoned for reasons beyond
PG&E’s control (Abandoned Plant or Abandonment Incentive); and (2) include 100% of
the Construction Work In Progress (CWIP) in transmission rate base during the
construction period (CWIP Incentive) for nine of the thirteen projects.

           As demonstrated below, and in the declarations and materials submitted as
attachments to this Petition, these two incentives are narrowly tailored to address the
demonstrable risks and challenges faced by PG&E constructing thirteen projects with an
estimated cost range of $1.7 billion to $3.3 billion.
          PG&E’s request is designed to support the timely and cost-effective development
of thirteen PG&E Projects needed to maintain reliability and serve forecasted load
growth. The requested incentives address two distinct barriers: the risk that PG&E will
incur significant, prudently incurred costs before a project is potentially cancelled for
reasons beyond its control, and the financing and customer rate impacts associated with
funding long-duration construction before assets enter service. Together, the incentives
will provide the regulatory certainty necessary to make timely project commitments,
reduce total financing costs borne by customers, and mitigate the concentration of rate
impacts as multiple projects enter service between 2031 and 2034.
          Moreover, given PG&E’s credit rating, which is lower than a typical utility, 5 the
Abandonment and CWIP Incentives are especially important for PG&E to efficiently
finance and construct these projects. In addition to providing upfront regulatory
certainty, rate stability, and improved cash flow, the incentives requested by PG&E will
also benefit customers. As described in more detail below, customers will incur lower
financing costs and, as a result of the CWIP Incentive, will be expected to pay millions of
dollars less in gross revenue over the projects’ lives.
          Finally, PG&E is requesting approval within sixty days of this request because
work will start shortly on the PG&E Projects, and PG&E must now make substantial
commitments for long lead-time equipment needed to complete construction according to

          The PG&E Projects face many challenges that are outside of PG&E’s control as
described in Section III. Given the substantial cost of the PG&E Projects (up to $3.3
billion, in aggregate), the time needed to perform this work (an estimated six to nine
years, at a minimum), the long-lead time required to order equipment, the risks and
challenges faced (e.g., permitting, regulatory approvals, construction challenges, and
many others), and that PG&E can invest up to $20 billion in electric transmission
investment between 2026 and 2030, the Abandonment and CWIP Incentives are critical
to provide upfront regulatory certainty, rate stability, and improved cash flow.7
Moreover, these incentives will ultimately lower customer costs. PG&E has narrowly
tailored its request in this Petition to those incentives that are most appropriate following
careful consideration of key characteristics of the PG&E Projects. Indeed, of these
thirteen CAISO TPP projects, PG&E is only seeking the CWIP Incentive for nine of the
projects where PG&E viewed the need as greatest after assessing timelines, costs, and
associated risks. Therefore, given the facts and circumstances described below, the
Commission should approve PG&E’s request.

purpose of recovering rate incentives associated with the Projects. 8 Specifically, for the
Abandonment Incentive, if the PG&E Projects are cancelled or abandoned for reasons
outside PG&E’s control, PG&E will make a Section 205 filing to recover 100% of its
prudently incurred costs. For the CWIP Incentive, PG&E will include the PG&E

Annual Updates that are submitted to the Commission by no later than December 1 of

II.       BACKGROUND
          A.      Description of PG&E
          PG&E is a California corporation and a wholly-owned subsidiary of PG&E
Corporation. PG&E is an investor-owned utility regulated by the California Public
Utilities Commission (CPUC), the Commission, and a number of other federal and state
agencies or governmental entities. PG&E is the principal provider of electric and gas
transmission and distribution service in northern and central California and is a
participating transmission owner (PTO) in the CAISO. As a PTO, PG&E has an
obligation to perform projects approved in the CAISO’s Transmission Plan that are
located in PG&E’s service territory.
          B.      Description of the CAISO 2025-2026 Transmission Plan

potential system limitations as well as opportunities for system improvement by

          A.      Common Risks and Challenges Facing Each of the Thirteen Projects

challenges, such as federal, state, and local agency review. For some of these projects,
PG&E will be required to secure certificates of public convenience and necessity (CPCN)
from the CPUC, including review under the California Environmental Quality Act. The
CPUC process to obtain a CPCN is a lengthy and complex process and involves two

         B.      Saratoga – Vasona 230 kilovolt (kV) line Reconductoring Project
          The Saratoga – Vasona 230 kV line Reconductoring Project was approved as a
reliability project. Planning studies indicate that with ongoing load growth in the Bay
Area, the lower-rated Saratoga-Vasona circuit between Metcalf-Monta vista corridor is
expected to overload under contingency conditions. As the studies showed, under a North
American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC TPL-001-5) category P6 event
involving the loss of two high-capacity circuits, the Saratoga-Vasona 230 kV line is
overloaded. 17

         D.         Monta Vista 230/115kV Transformer Bank Addition Project
          The Monta Vista 230/115kV Transformer Bank Addition Project was approved as
a reliability project. The three existing 230/115 kV transformer banks at the Monta Vista
substation primarily supply power to the De Anza 115 kV system. Additional sources for
this area include the 230/115 kV transformer banks located at the Newark and
Ravenswood substations. On the 230 kV side, the Monta Vista substation is connected
solely to Metcalf via four lines. In the 115 kV network, there are two double circuits that
link this substation to Ravenswood and Newark. According to load forecasts for the De
Anza division, the area is expected to experience significant load growth, increasing from
480 MW in 2027 to 730 MW in 2040, which includes overall continued Bay Area load
growth, along the 115 kV path from Monta Vista to Newark. Power flow studies indicate
that if any two of the three 230/115 kV transformers are out of service, particularly under
P6 contingencies, most of the load in the De Anza area would still be supported by the
remaining transformers, resulting in its overload by 2035. 23

being requested), and the in-service date may be pushed back if there are delays or there

make substantial commitments in 2026 and cash outlays in later years for equipment, but
will not be able to recover these costs until several years after the commitments and costs
are incurred. 105 In the absence of the CWIP Incentive, PG&E’s investors would have to
wait up to five years (i.e., 2031, when the some of the PG&E Projects will go in service)

comparison with other PG&E investments which have shorter lead-times and thus

          To satisfy the nexus test, an applicant must demonstrate that the total package of
incentives requested is tailored to address the demonstrable risks and challenges faced. 125
The Commission has “approved multiple rate incentives for particular projects where
appropriate as long as each incentive is justified by a showing that it satisfies the
requirements of Section 219 and is appropriate.” 126 The Commission has frequently
approved both Abandonment and CWIP Incentives for large transmission projects. 127
          In this case, PG&E’s request is narrowly tailored to address the risks and

the need for upfront regulatory certainty, rate stability, and improved cash flow and thus

I.   OVERVIEW OF THE CAISO’S 2025-2026 TPP

6.   The CAISO’s 2025-2026 TPP began in January 2025 and concluded in May 2026.
     The CAISO Board of Governors subsequently approved updates to the Plan in
     August 2026. The TPP generally consists of the following three phases:

     • Phase 1: During this phase, the CAISO develops the Unified Planning
        Assumptions and a Study Plan that provides the scope and details of the
        technical studies to be conducted in the planning cycle. The CAISO also
        begins development of a conceptual statewide plan that would be considered as
        an input into the CAISO comprehensive plan.

     • Phase 2: This phase usually occurs over a 14-month period during which the
        technical studies are conducted. At the end of this phase, the comprehensive
        Transmission Plan, which describes the study results and identifies
        transmission projects and transmission elements, is developed. Phase 2 is
        completed when the CAISO’s management presents the comprehensive
        Transmission Plan to the CAISO’s Board of Governors for approval and the
        CAISO Board of Governors approves a Final Transmission Plan.

     • Phase 3: This phase is undertaken if Transmission Plan elements eligible for
        competitive solicitation are approved by the CAISO Board of Governors at the

         and own specified elements included in the comprehensive Transmission Plan.
         The CAISO evaluates the proposals and selects the PG&E project sponsor to
         construct and own the transmission upgrades or additional elements. The
         CAISO’s competitive solicitation process applies to all regional transmission
         solutions. The only exception to the competitive solicitation process is a
         solution involving modifications to existing facilities. Because CAISO did not
         identify any of the thirteen PG&E Projects described in this declaration as
         eligible for Phase 3 competitive solicitation, none of these projects were
         included in Phase 3 of the 2025-2026 TPP.

7.    Phase 2 of the 2025-2026 TPP was completed in May 2026, when the CAISO

      CAISO Board approved the 2025-2026 Transmission Plan in May 2026, which
      included a total of thirty-seven transmission projects, and later approved updates
      to the 2025-2026 Transmission Plan in August 2026. Thirteen of the approved
      projects assigned to PG&E are included in this declaration.

8.    These projects were identified by the CAISO as necessary to ensure the reliability
      of the transmission system and deliverability of renewable and energy storage
      resources into the CAISO-controlled grid.

II.   OVERVIEW OF THE THIRTEEN PROJECTS

9.    CAISO’s 2025–2026 TPP Phase 2 identified the need for these thirteen projects

III.   NEEDS IDENTIFIED IN TPP

10.    The thirteen PG&E Projects were determined by the CAISO in Phase 2 of the
       2025–2026 TPP to be necessary for the reasons set out below.

11.    Saratoga – Vasona 230 kilovolt (kV) line Reconductoring Project: The Saratoga –
       Vasona 230 kV line Reconductoring Project was approved as a reliability project.

       a North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC TPL-001-5) category

       kV line is overloaded.

12.    Tesla – Trimble – Metcalf 230 kV Corridor Expansion Project: The Tesla –

          57% as of August 2026. This reflects investor concerns regarding the risk of
          wildfires in the state of California and currently limits PG&E’s access to equity
          capital at a reasonable cost.

15.       Elevated wildfire risk coupled with California's current wildfire liability
          framework results in higher financing costs which are ultimately borne by
          customers. 8 During the 2026 California legislative session, California lawmakers
          failed to pass Senate Bill (SB) 492, so California does not have the long-term
          durability needed to attract affordable investment to support a safer, more reliable
          energy system and help keep down costs for customers. 9. Under California’s
          existing framework, utilities such as PG&E act as uncompensated insurers of last
          resort in the event of catastrophic wildfires, 10 translating wildfire risk into higher
          financing costs and limiting PG&E’s ability to affordably fund its energy system.
          The recent legislative outcome maintains a risk profile for California investor
          owned utilities that contributes to suppressed credit ratings and elevated financing
          costs.

16.       Financing the PG&E Projects will place greater stress on PG&E’s balance sheet
          and have negative effects on PG&E’s cash flow and financial metrics. This is
          because the total combined investment in the PG&E Projects and PG&E’s other

       electric transmission infrastructure projects comprise a multi-billion-dollar figure

17.    Investors will view risk and reward of the PG&E Projects in light of PG&E’s total
       electric transmission spending, as well as its overall capital spending. As
       discussed previously, PG&E plans to invest up to $20 billion in electric
       transmission investments during a portion of the PG&E Projects’ construction
       period (i.e., 2026-2030).

18.    In addition to PG&E’s forecasted infrastructure spending, investors will also
       consider specific electric transmission project risks. Generally and unlike the
       PG&E Projects described herein, PG&E’s standard transmission investments are
       undertaken to replace or maintain existing infrastructure, and do not face the same
       heightened execution risk due to multiple jurisdictional approvals with significant
       environmental reviews and permitting. These more standard transmission
       investments can often be completed in less time, and are less likely to be
       abandoned or canceled.

19.    PG&E anticipates the PG&E Projects will incur significant commitments for
       equipment, with construction costs to follow for projects being placed in service
       between 2031 and 2034, at the earliest. In the absence of the CWIP Incentive,
       PG&E’s investors would have to wait years before receiving any cash return of or
       on their investment. All things equal, this long delay diminishes the attractiveness
       of this investment in comparison with other investments that have shorter lead-
       times and, thus, provide a cash return more quickly.


III.   PG&E’S REQUESTED INCENTIVES SATISFY THE NEXUS TEST

20.   As indicated above, PG&E’s Petition requests two incentives – the Abandoned
      Plant Incentive and the CWIP Incentive. As explained below, both incentives are
      tailored to address PG&E’s demonstrable risks or challenges.


      A. ABANDONED PLANT INCENTIVE

21.   The Abandoned Plant Incentive is critical because, without it, PG&E could incur
      substantial costs and expenses which would not be fully recoverable in rates if the
      PG&E Projects are abandoned through no fault of PG&E. The risk of
      abandonment is especially acute here because of the numerous variables outside of
      PG&E’s control—described in detail in Exhibit A—that could cause any or all of
      the PG&E projects to be abandoned or cancelled by the CAISO. Investors
      consider the risk of not being able to recover their investment and, in a case such
      as this, there is a substantial risk of abandonment.

22.   The Abandoned Plant Incentive effectively addresses this investor risk by ensuring
      that PG&E can recover 100 percent of its prudently incurred costs if Projects are
      cancelled or abandoned for reasons beyond PG&E’s control. Therefore, the
      Commission should grant PG&E’s request for the Abandoned Plant Incentive for
      the PG&E Projects.


      B. CWIP INCENTIVE

23.   The CWIP Incentive is also narrowly tailored to address PG&E’s risks and
      challenges. Including CWIP in rate base will improve cash flow at a time when
      PG&E is preparing to finance a expansion and upgrade of its system.

24.   PG&E’s planned electric transmission investment through 2030 is substantial (i.e.,
      approximately $20 billion), and this spending coincides with significant need for

      wildfire-mitigation-related capital expenditures, growth in PG&E’s distribution
      capital investments, and infrastructure replacements required to support system
      reliability. Thus, increased cash flow prior to the in-service date of the PG&E
      Projects will support PG&E’s credit quality as it expends large amounts of capital
      during this period. Ultimately, degraded credit quality leads to higher borrowing
      costs, which would be borne by PG&E’s customers.

25.   As PG&E undertakes large and lengthy construction projects, CWIP and
      Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (AFUDC) balances will increase
      based on the cash requirements of these projects. When CWIP balances are high
      and AFUDC comprises a major portion of earnings, investors become concerned
      about the quality of earnings, subsequent rate shock (when the PG&E projects are
      added to rate base), and the ability of the utility to generate a prompt return of, and
      on, invested capital. Including CWIP in rate base will assist PG&E with its
      financing requirements and credit rating agency coverage ratios by replacing non-
      cash AFUDC with cash revenues. In addition, credit ratings are supported due to
      better financial metrics. The utility’s stronger credit profile due to less borrowing
      will allow for lower financing costs, which will ultimately benefit customers.

26.   Moreover, collection of rate of return revenue on CWIP under CWIP Incentive
      ratemaking can offset the need for traditional capital market financing, which
      could carry relatively higher costs for customers in high-interest rate
      environments. Customers benefit when higher cost borrowings are replaced by
      operational cash flows from revenue, all else equal.

27.   Further, CWIP Incentive ratemaking can potentially result in the collection of less
      revenue from customers over the life of the PG&E Projects relative to standard
      ratemaking, and mitigate rate shock. This is generally driven by the absence of
